title: Arjuna's austerities
hook: the warrior becomes an ascetic, eating less and less, until the sages of the mountain go to Shiva about him

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna's austerities began with a test: Indra, in disguise, told him to throw away his bow, and he wouldn't. Your line was remember why you came. Did you name your why before you started something? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

A warrior in grass clothes. That's what the sages on the mountain see when they look at the newcomer. Arjuna, prince and archer, has traded his royal dress for rags of grass and a deerskin, and taken up a staff. He's come to the foot of the Himalayas to do one thing: to draw the attention of Shiva. And the way he sets about it is tapas, the slow, burning work of austerity. Today, what Arjuna's austerities actually looked like, and what they did to the mountain.
screen: `A WARRIOR IN GRASS CLOTHES.` → `TO DRAW SHIVA'S ATTENTION.` → `THE BURNING WORK OF TAPAS.`

segments.voice: The epic describes it step by step. At first Arjuna eats fruit, but only every few nights. Then less often. Then less. Month by month he narrows his life, until at last he lives on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes with his arms raised, motionless. His hair, the text says, grows matted and bright. Now here's the strange part. His austerity isn't quiet. It gives off heat. In this story, tapas burns, and the burning is real. The sages who live on the mountain begin to feel it. Smoke, in the epic's telling, seems to rise from the earth around him. They grow worried. So they go to Shiva and say, more or less: who is this man, and what is he doing? His austerity is troubling us all. Shiva's answer is calm. Don't worry, he says. I know what's in Arjuna's heart. I know what he wants. Go back, and be at peace. So while Arjuna stands on his toes with his arms in the air, the god he came to find already knows what he's after. Arjuna hasn't said a word to Shiva. His discipline has spoken for him, loudly enough that the neighbors went to complain. On this mountain, at least, practice isn't private.
screen: `LESS FOOD, THEN ONLY AIR.` · `TAPAS GIVES OFF HEAT.` · `THE SAGES GO TO SHIVA.` · then, large: `SHIVA ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand, and let the body be still in whatever way is comfortable. You don't need to stand on your toes. Just notice the warmth of your own body: in the hands, the chest, the face. Breathe in, and feel that warmth. Breathe out, and let it settle. Bring to mind one small discipline you keep, or would like to keep. As you breathe, let it feel less like a burden and more like a little heat you carry. If you pray, you can offer that discipline in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's austerities. Less food, then only air, a heat the sages felt, and a god who already knew what he wanted.
Your line: keep discipline without announcing it. Today, keep one small discipline without announcing it, and trust that it's doing its work anyway. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Tapas, disciplined austerity such as fasting, stillness and self-restraint, runs through Hindu stories and practice; Arjuna on the mountain is one of the epic's pictures of a seeker whose tapas draws a god's response.

original.note: Sanskrit tapas: disciplined austerity, which in the stories gives off heat.

trapdoor: what you thought: austerity is a private thing you do alone.
what it means: Arjuna's tapas changes the mountain, and the sages feel it and go to Shiva.
what a scholar hears: in the story, the discipline called tapas gives off real heat, and the smoking ground makes it visible.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Kairata Parva (Arjuna's austerities in the Himalaya; the sages go to Shiva; Shiva reassures them)

notes: All paraphrase. Ganguli gives the stages month by month with specific intervals; the script gives them without numbers under the claims rule. Confirm the progression and the final stage (living on air, arms raised, on tiptoe).
Confirm the descriptions of his dress (grass, deerskin, staff), of his matted hair, and of smoke rising from the earth.
Confirm that the sages describe his tapas as troubling them and that Shiva says he knows Arjuna's desire.
'Tapas' meaning 'heat' is standard Sanskrit (the root tap, to heat); Keeper to confirm it's acceptable under the etymology rule.
